items.title: Al Rose Interview, 1975-02-03
items.q: [INTERVIEWER] Oh yeah. And I was interviewing Bill Russell last night and he was talking about the masters that he rejected years ago, so I'm great now. [INTERVIEWEE] Oh sure. Well, of course your criteria change...

ctx.x: What's your name anyway? My name is Al Rose. Is that your full name? No, my full name is H.N. Alphonse Delarose Lascaux. My God. I thought it was E. Albert Rose for years. Well, I actually did use that name for years for complex reasons. Where were you born? I was born in New Orleans in a 2-0 infirmary on February 3rd, 1916. Makes me 59 years old today. Just,

I'm not taking anything in any particular order. Okay. Other than happy birthday. Thank you, Richard. Oh, I didn't tell you my name. My name is Dick Allen, commonly known as Richard. Enough of this feeble attempt at you, and I'm tired. I interviewed Russell last night. Two hours of tennis and one hour of interview with Russell. It's an hour and a half. What I did with Russell. That's the D-In for a whole day. Where have you been a disc jockey? Well, I

wouldn't exactly think of myself as a disc jockey. I did, of course, run the radio show Journeys Into Jazz, which began in 1946 in Philadelphia, and is now syndicated through Southern Illinois University Radio Network. And it's just a mini-series of programs about jazz and jazz musicians on which records are played for illustration. What station was this in Philadelphia? WFIL, ABC. They had a little Eastern network that covered a lot of ABC affiliates in the area, and I had a pretty big audience back in the 40s.…

items.title: Betty Lee Hanson, Joe James, George Lewis, Joe Lewis, Joe Butler, Kid Thomas Valentine, Bill Russell, Allan…
items.q: And this is one of our friends, Al Rose, is trying to get a certain definition adopted...

ctx.x: Well, what about this pure jazz that all of you are trying to preserve?

Well, there may be a little difference, a little difference in the feeling of the white and the colored. It's hard to put your finger on it, though, and say definitely, because some of the white musicians undoubtedly played the same style as the colored in the old days. Maybe the colored held on to that old time feeling a little bit better, a little bit longer than the white musicians. But today, they all call it, for instance, Dixieland. A lot of people try to make a big point between what they call New Orleans…
Well, which came first, the colored movement towards ragtime and blues or the white movement towards ragtime and blues, or were they simultaneous?

items.title: Al Rose Interview, 1976-02-19
items.q: I would say that if you were going to make a comparison between Russell and me with respect to our general approaches to it... Probably nobody has the direct relationship, certainly, to the black jazz or the black musicians seen in lives in Russell.

ctx.x: Let me mention another name here. Do you think that someone, for instance, like Bill Russell, who's a musician himself, a classical violinist, knows something about the nature of jazz?
Oh, he certainly does. Bill Russell is a genuine jazz authority. And, of course, his, you know...
And I was going to ask you whether he agrees with you on your theory of jazz.
